title: First Eastern Europe, now Libya: The Ukraine war expands its reach
text:
First Eastern Europe, now Libya: The Ukraine war expands its reach
More sophisticated military technology developed by Ukraine, and suspected Russian message-sending, are expanding the borders of the Ukraine war.
Ukraine demonstrated the reach and effectiveness of the war machine it has developed since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 with weekend attacks on Russian vessels docked in Libya.
The strikes – carried out Sunday by Ukrainian sea drones – sank one ship, heavily damaged another, and destroyed a Russian combat helicopter.
The attacks in the eastern Mediterranean followed by two days the strikes on Polish territory by two Russian missiles and one drone. Together the military operations put an exclamation mark on a geographical expansion of Russia’s war on Ukraine that has been simmering for more than a year – primarily with Russian cyber and drone attacks on Eastern European members of NATO.
In nearly five years of war, Ukraine has developed the ability to strike deeper into Russia, as well as hit Russian targets farther afield. Russian drones and missiles also hit beyond Ukrainian territory. Together, they are expanding the war’s geography.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed Monday that Ukrainian sea drones had carried out the Libya attacks. He also insisted that the attacks’ targets were military material. Russia has been building up its military links in eastern Libya since losing its bases in Syria in 2024.
“We are responding to Russia’s aggression,” Mr. Zelenskyy said in a social media post. Referring to Ukraine’s unmatched drones and its innovative sea drones, he said, “We are developing Ukrainian weapons.”
The Libya attacks illustrate the rapid advance of Ukraine’s military technology, analysts say.
“Ukraine is at the cutting edge of sea drone technology. What they are doing with drone warfare while under attack from Russia is extraordinary,” says Bradley Bowman, senior director of the Center on Military and Political Power at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies in Washington. “There’s nothing like the worst invasion in Europe since World War II to concentrate the mind to do what you need to do to defend your country.”
Also Monday, Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo implied on the social media platform X that it was Ukrainian drones that had set ablaze a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday.
“War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity,” Mr. Orpo said, adding, “Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”
Mr. Bowman says Russia, Europe, and Washington are learning that “what begins in Ukraine will not stay in Ukraine.”
The missile and drone strikes on Polish territory were set to be discussed at a meeting Monday in Brussels of NATO’s high-level North Atlantic Council. In remarks to journalists Saturday in Warsaw, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte condemned the attacks and vowed that the Alliance “will defend every inch of Polish territory.”
Polish defense officials noted that while none of the Russian strikes caused death or serious injury, they underscored that all three attacks took place near a military training ground where forces from 11 countries are participating in joint exercises.
For Mr. Bowman at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies, Russia’s strikes on NATO territory are a message. “[Russian President Vladimir] Putin resents NATO and its member states not because NATO is a threat to him, but because a country that is a NATO member is less easy for him to bully.”
The alarm among NATO’s European partners contrasts with the response from U.S. President Donald Trump, who downplayed the attacks, saying only that Russia “has been landing drones in Poland, and a couple of little missiles, by mistake.”
The comments came days after Mr. Trump’s meetings with the Russian president – whom he referred to as “my friend” – in China last week. After those meetings Mr. Trump told European leaders that Mr. Putin “wants to end the war, he wants the deal done.”
European leaders including French President Emmanuel Macron and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said after Mr. Trump’s comment that Europe is ready for talks to end the war as well – as long as Europe has an equal role at the negotiating table.
